title: The Rubik's Cube Episode
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Rubik's Cube: its invention by Hungarian architecture professor Ernő Rubik (originally the Bévüs kocka or "magic cube"), the Tibor Laczi deal that brought it to Ideal Toy Company at the Nuremberg Toy Fair, its 1980s craze and solution books, the cube's mechanics and the roughly 43 quintillion configurations, algorithms and the story of how Rubik solved his own puzzle, speed cubing and world championships (including the Red Bull sponsorship and the World Cube Association), God's number, the Larry Nichols and Molecular Research patent litigation, and Rubik's later life. The episode closes with listener mail correcting the pronunciation of "Sanskrit" and the coconut tree discussion from a previous episode.
topics: Red Bull Rubik's Cube World Championship

entities.name: The Simple Solution to Rubik's Cube

segments.title: Opening banter and Rubik the Amazing Cube
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with a cartoon clip reference to Rubik the Amazing Cube, a Chicago show plug, and casual talk about the cube's popularity and their own experiences solving it.

segments.title: What the Rubik's Cube is and its origins
segments.summary: The hosts describe the cube's structure of smaller cubies and its colored faces, note its National Toy Hall of Fame induction in 2014, and explain it was invented in 1974 by Hungarian architecture professor Ernő Rubik, originally called the Bűvös kocka (magic cube).

segments.title: Tibor Laczi and the deal with Ideal Toy
segments.summary: The cube sold locally in Hungary before Tibor Laczi bought one from a restaurant waiter, met Rubik, and took it to toy fairs. At the Nuremberg Toy Fair he met people tied to Ideal Toy Company, which bought the global rights and renamed it the Rubik's Cube.

segments.title: The 1980s craze, sales, and solution books
segments.summary: Sales reached hundreds of millions, awards followed, and solution books topped the New York Times bestseller list, including James G. Nourse's The Simple Solution to Rubik's Cube and a book by 12-year-old Patrick Bossert. The hosts also mention cubist's thumb, a tendonitis described in a medical journal.
topics: The Simple Solution to Rubik's Cube

segments.title: How Rubik designed the mechanism and solved his own puzzle
segments.summary: Rubik reportedly began the design as a model for a 3D design class, and the mechanical solution (a central sphere with arms and rotating pieces) came to him on the Danube. Coloring the cube made it a puzzle, and he took about a month to work out solution algorithms.

segments.title: Configurations, algorithms, and notation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the roughly 43 quintillion possible configurations, the single solved state, the use of algorithms and move notation from solution books, and why the puzzle is learnable through memorized sequences.

segments.title: Speed cubing and world championships
segments.summary: Countries held national championships the year after the cube's release, followed by the first World Championship in Budapest. The hosts discuss speed records, the 2018 record of 3.47 seconds by Yu Shang Yu, the 2003 Toronto competition by Dan Gosby, and specialized speed cubes with magnets.

segments.title: Red Bull sponsorship and the World Cube Association
segments.summary: The hosts discuss corporate sponsorship of cubing events by Red Bull, the grassroots World Cube Association, and the renaming of the sponsored event as the World Cup to avoid conflict.
topics: Red Bull Rubik's Cube World Championship

segments.title: God's number and the Devil's number
segments.summary: The hosts explain God's number, the maximum moves needed to solve any configuration, estimated around 20 using computer analysis, and mention the Devil's number concept for traversing all configurations.

segments.title: Patent dispute with Larry Nichols
segments.summary: Larry Nichols held a 1972 US patent on a similar 2x2x2 cube and sued via Molecular Research Corporation. A court ruled for them, but an appeals court overturned it in 1986 and another upheld that in 1989. Frank Fox's 1974 patent had lapsed. Nichols reportedly said the settlement helped send his kids to Harvard.

segments.title: Ernő Rubik today and related puzzles
segments.summary: Rubik is still alive, teaches architecture in Hungary, and runs foundations. The hosts mention larger cubes, the Snake, the S Cube, and the films Cube and The Pursuit of Happyness.

segments.title: Listener mail: Sanskrit pronunciation and coconut tree
segments.summary: A listener corrects the pronunciation of Sanskrit and adds context about the kalpavriksha coconut tree from a previous episode, and asks about pronunciation of non-Western words.
